units.t: Reading Like a Writer: Literary Analysis

learn: Literary analysis explains how an author creates meaning, not just what happens.
An analytical claim is arguable and specific: "Through recurring images of light, the author suggests that knowledge both reveals and burns."
High school analysis moves from plot summary to the author's choices and their effects.
lessons.try: Rewrite three summary sentences as analytical claims.

learn: Writers make deliberate choices in diction (word choice), syntax (sentence structure), imagery and structure.
Ask of every choice: what effect does this have on the reader, and why might the author have chosen it?
Short sentences can create tension; long, flowing ones can create calm or overwhelm.
lessons.try: Analyse the diction and syntax of one paragraph from a classic short story.

learn: A strong body paragraph has a topic sentence (claim), evidence, analysis and a concluding link to the thesis.
Analysis should be longer than the quotation it discusses.
Avoid "This quote shows..."; instead name the technique and its effect.
check: Analysis should usually be ___ than the quote.
A better phrase than "This quote shows" names the...
lessons.try: Write one analytical paragraph with embedded evidence.

units.t: The Short Story: Plot, Character and Point of View

learn: Freytag's pyramid: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution.
Many modern stories begin in medias res (in the middle of the action).
Pacing controls tension through scene length and detail.
check: In the middle of the action
lessons.try: Map Saki's "The Open Window" (1914) on Freytag's pyramid.

learn: Complex characters have multiple or conflicting motivations.
Static characters stay the same; dynamic characters change.
Foils are characters who contrast with the protagonist to highlight traits.
lessons.try: Identify a foil in a story and explain what it reveals.

learn: First-person narrators may be unreliable: biased, naive or deceptive.
Third-person limited follows one character's thoughts; omniscient knows all.
Poe's narrator in "The Cask of Amontillado" (1846) reveals more about himself than he intends.
check: "The Cask of Amontillado" was written by...
lessons.try: Find three clues that a narrator is unreliable.

learn: A symbol is a concrete object, person or action that represents an abstract idea.
Symbols gain meaning through repetition and context.
In Nathaniel Hawthorne's "The Minister's Black Veil" (1836), the veil symbolises hidden sin.
lessons.try: Track a symbol through a story and explain how its meaning develops.

learn: Setting can reflect characters' inner states or social conditions.
Gothic settings (decaying houses, storms) create dread.
Setting can act almost as an antagonist.
lessons.try: Analyse how setting builds mood in Poe's "The Fall of the House of Usher".

learn: A theme is the text's insight about life, stated as a complete idea.
Combine evidence from character, symbol and setting to support a thematic claim.
Avoid clichés; state themes with nuance.
check: A theme is an insight about...
lessons.try: Write a thesis about theme using two literary elements.

units.t: Poetry: Imagery, Figurative Language and Form

learn: Imagery appeals to the senses; figurative language includes metaphor, simile, personification, metonymy and synecdoche.
Synecdoche uses a part for the whole ("all hands on deck").
Percy Bysshe Shelley's "Ozymandias" (1818) uses images of ruin to comment on power.
lessons.try: Analyse the imagery of "Ozymandias" and its irony.

learn: The Shakespearean sonnet has three quatrains and a couplet (ABAB CDCD EFEF GG).
The Petrarchan sonnet has an octave and a sestet with a volta (turn).
Form shapes how an argument or feeling unfolds.
check: A Shakespearean sonnet ends with a...
The turn in a sonnet is the...
A Petrarchan sonnet has an octave and a...
lessons.try: Mark the volta in a Petrarchan sonnet.

learn: Use TP-CASTT: Title, Paraphrase, Connotation, Attitude, Shifts, Title again, Theme.
Read aloud to hear sound and rhythm.
Emily Dickinson's "Because I could not stop for Death" (1890) personifies Death as a gentleman caller.
check: In TP-CASTT, the S stands for...
lessons.try: Apply TP-CASTT to the Dickinson poem.

learn: "Romeo and Juliet" (about 1595) is a tragedy set in Verona about two young lovers from feuding families.
The Prologue is a sonnet that reveals the ending: the "star-crossed lovers" will die.
Revealing the ending creates dramatic irony throughout.
check: The Prologue is written as a...
lessons.try: Paraphrase the Prologue line by line.

learn: Shakespeare uses blank verse (unrhymed iambic pentameter) for nobles and prose for servants and comic moments.
Romeo's speech shifts from clichéd love poetry for Rosaline to vivid imagery for Juliet.
Mercutio's wit and the Nurse's rambling reveal character.
lessons.try: Compare Romeo's language about Rosaline and about Juliet.

learn: The play balances fate against characters' hasty choices.
A tragic flaw contributes to downfall; for Romeo, perhaps impulsiveness.
The deaths reconcile the feuding families.
check: The deaths lead the families to...
lessons.try: Write an argument: is fate or choice more responsible for the ending?

learn: An epic is a long narrative poem about a hero's journey, often involving gods.
Homer's "Odyssey" (about the 700s BCE) follows Odysseus's ten-year voyage home after the Trojan War.
Epics begin with an invocation of the Muse and use epithets ("grey-eyed Athena").
check: Epics begin with an invocation of the...
lessons.try: Find three epithets in the opening of the "Odyssey".

learn: Odysseus's defining trait is cunning, shown in tricking the Cyclops Polyphemus.
His pride, shouting his name to the Cyclops, brings Poseidon's anger.
The epic hero archetype mixes great virtues and flaws.
lessons.try: Chart Odysseus's virtues and flaws in three episodes.

learn: Penelope, Odysseus's wife, shows loyalty and cleverness, delaying suitors by weaving and unweaving a shroud.
Themes include hospitality (xenia), loyalty, perseverance and the cost of pride.
The "Odyssey" introduced the word "odyssey" for any long journey.
lessons.try: Explain the role of xenia in two episodes.

learn: SOAPSTone: Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject, Tone.
Understanding the situation explains the author's choices.
Patrick Henry's "Give me liberty or give me death" speech (1775) was delivered to the Virginia Convention.
check: Purpose refers to what the speaker...
lessons.try: Apply SOAPSTone to Patrick Henry's speech.

learn: Anaphora repeats words at the start of clauses; parallelism uses similar structures.
Rhetorical questions make a point without expecting answers.
Antithesis contrasts ideas in balanced phrases: "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times."
check: Repeating words at the start of clauses is...
"The best of times, the worst of times" is...
lessons.try: Find three rhetorical devices in a famous speech.

learn: Evaluate claims, reasoning and evidence; look for fallacies.
Common fallacies: straw man, slippery slope, hasty generalisation, appeal to authority.
Consider what the author leaves out.
check: Misrepresenting an opponent's argument is a...
"If we allow this, disaster will follow" can be a...
Judging from too few examples is...
lessons.try: Identify fallacies in a set of editorials.

learn: A defensible thesis takes a position and previews reasons.
A line of reasoning connects claims logically from paragraph to paragraph.
Each body paragraph advances the argument rather than repeating it.
lessons.try: Write a thesis and outline three reasons.

learn: Integrate quotations with signal phrases and explain them.
Use MLA in-text citations: (Author page).
Paraphrasing must change both words and structure and still be cited.
lessons.try: Write a paragraph integrating two sources with MLA citations.

learn: Concede a valid point, then rebut: "Although critics argue..., the evidence shows..."
Revise for clarity, concision and logical flow.
Peer review with specific questions improves drafts.
lessons.try: Revise an argumentative essay after peer review.

learn: A run-on joins independent clauses without proper punctuation.
A comma splice joins them with only a comma.
Fix with a period, semicolon, or comma plus coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS).
lessons.try: Fix ten run-ons and comma splices.

learn: Parallel structure uses the same grammatical form: "She likes hiking, swimming and reading."
Subjects and verbs agree in number: "The box of apples is heavy."
Pronouns agree with their antecedents.
lessons.try: Correct sentences with faulty parallelism.

learn: Formal academic style avoids contractions, slang and second person.
Vary sentence openings and lengths.
Strong verbs replace weak verb-adverb pairs: "sprinted" instead of "ran quickly".
lessons.try: Revise a paragraph to strengthen its style.

learn: Track plot, character, theme and symbols in a reading journal.
Mary Shelley's "Frankenstein" (1818) explores ambition, responsibility and what makes us human.
Discuss with others to deepen understanding.
lessons.try: Keep a reading journal for a public-domain novel.

learn: Develop a research question, find credible sources, take notes and synthesise.
Use academic databases and library resources.
Synthesis combines sources to create new insight rather than listing them.
lessons.try: Write an annotated bibliography of five sources.

learn: Present findings clearly with a thesis, evidence and visuals.
Cite sources in a works cited list.
Practise delivery: eye contact, pace and volume.
lessons.try: Present a five-minute research talk connecting a novel to its historical context.
